rationale: Start with a broad gradient to locate the six-compound elution window and identify critical pairs while minimizing the risk of missing retained compounds. A moderate temperature leaves room to probe temperature-dependent selectivity in either direction.

The first method already achieves the maximum CRF, with ample resolution margin. Shorten the gradient while holding the solvent window and temperature fixed to test whether full resolution can be retained in a faster run.
Reduce the gradient by one grid step to seek a still faster fully resolved method. The closest pair remains at R = 2.46 in the six-minute gradient, leaving some margin for further compression.

The four-minute gradient retains maximum CRF but leaves little resolution margin for the closest pair. Raise temperature one step to test whether retention can be shortened without pushing that pair below R = 1.5.

Return to 40 C to preserve the closest pair’s selectivity, and raise the starting organic fraction to trim the low-organic portion of the gradient. The narrower window gives a shallower slope at the same gradient duration and may shorten retention while maintaining full resolution.

Test the shortest programmable gradient at lower temperature, since warming reduced the critical pair’s resolution. Cooling may recover enough selectivity to preserve full resolution while the shorter gradient reduces the last-peak time.

Raise the starting organic fraction to narrow the gradient window while retaining the strong final wash. The shallower slope may lift the critical pair above R = 1.5 and shorten the last-peak time; the main risk is compression of the earliest peaks.
The two-minute gradient achieves maximum CRF at 25 C. Raise temperature one step to test for a shorter last-peak time while checking whether the critical pair retains R ≥ 1.5.

Increase phi0 one grid step to make the gradient shallower and potentially recover the small resolution deficit at 30 C. This also tests the upper starting-organic limit before the earliest peaks become insufficiently retained.
Test one temperature step above the fastest fully resolved method to locate its resolution limit. Keep phi0 fixed because the first peak is already close to the unretained region.

Reduce the final organic fraction to make the gradient shallower and test whether the critical pair recovers full resolution at 35 C. The last peak may move into the final hold, but the strong endpoint should keep retention comfortably below ten minutes.

The earliest pair barely responded to slope at phi0 = 0.30, suggesting it elutes too early to benefit much from the gradient. Lower the starting fraction and shift the same-width window downward to retain that pair longer and test whether full resolution is recovered.

Return to the fastest fully resolved gradient window and cool one step to increase the critical pair’s resolution margin. This tests a more robust maximum-CRF method with only a small expected increase in last-peak time.

Test one higher starting-organic step at the temperature giving the strongest early-pair separation. This probes whether the run can be shortened further, although the first peak may become insufficiently retained; injection 9 remains the fastest confirmed fully resolved method.

Lower phi0 to keep the first peak away from the unretained region, and reduce phi1 slightly to improve resolution over injection 8. This tests a fast alternative with better early retention while preserving a strong endpoint for the last compound.

Lower the endpoint one step from the fastest fully resolved method to test whether a slightly shallower gradient adds useful resolution margin. All compounds should still elute well within ten minutes, preserving maximum CRF if the early pair remains resolved.

Cool injection 15 by one step to improve the critical pair’s resolution while keeping the first peak away from the unretained region. Maximum CRF is already established; this tests a short alternative with greater separation margin.

Test the starting-organic step between injections 6 and 7 to find the lowest phi0 that preserves full resolution with the fastest gradient. This should retain the earliest peaks more strongly while keeping the last peak near 2.7 minutes.

Reduce the endpoint one step to improve the marginal R = 1.51 of injection 18 while retaining its well-retained first peak. This tests a maximum-CRF alternative with more resolution margin and only a modest expected increase in last-peak time.

Combine the starting fraction that gave the strongest early-pair separation with a slightly shallower gradient at 25 C. This tests additional resolution margin in a sub-three-minute separation; injection 9 remains the fastest confirmed maximum-CRF method.

Narrow the window one step from injection 15 to increase its modest early-pair resolution margin while keeping the first peak adequately retained. This tests another short maximum-CRF candidate; injection 9 remains the fastest confirmed fully resolved method.

Test the remaining endpoint step near the fastest maximum-CRF method to measure the tradeoff between early-pair resolution and last-peak time. The slightly shallower gradient should preserve full resolution with all peaks comfortably below ten minutes.

Cool injection 21 one step to test greater critical-pair resolution while keeping the first peak adequately retained. Maximum CRF is already reached, so this evaluates separation margin rather than a higher attainable score.

Raise phi0 one step from injection 23 to test a slightly faster separation with comparable resolution margin, as seen at the neighboring endpoints. Injection 9 remains the fastest confirmed maximum-CRF method.

Use the final injection to test a shallower variant of injection 19, aiming to improve critical-pair resolution while keeping the first peak well retained and the separation short. The maximum CRF is already secured; injection 9 remains the fastest confirmed fully resolved method.
